Question#2

Yes, the names stayed attached to their original values.
This matters because a score is only meaningful when it is tied to the right person. If the names did not follow their values, the sorted list might show 92 next to “Eli” when Eli actually scored 67. You would then name the wrong student as top performer, and any ranking, award, or grade built on that list would be wrong.

Question#3

sort() drops NA values without any warning. If you then report the “lowest score” from the sorted result, you are only looking at the non-missing values. The student whose score is missing might have scored lower than everyone else, or the data might be incomplete in a way that changes the conclusion. Because nothing signals that data was removed, you could report a minimum that looks valid but is misleading. You should check with is.na() or sum(is.na(x)) first, so you know how much data is missing.

Question#5

```{r}
name    <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")
score   <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
section <- c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")

students <- data.frame(name, score, section)
students
```
```{r}
students[order(students$score), ]

```
```{r}
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Question#6

order(scores) returns a vector of positions, not scores. In our example it gives 5 7 1 3 6 2 4. This means “the smallest value is in position 5, the next smallest is in position 7, then position 1,” and so on.
On its own this is not useful because it is only a list of index numbers. You cannot read it as scores or names. It becomes useful when you use it to index something, such as scores[order(scores)] or students[order(students$score), ], which rearranges the data into that order.

Question#7

sort() works on a single vector and returns only that vector’s sorted values. A data frame has several columns that belong together row by row. sort(students) has no clear meaning: should it sort each column independently, and by what rule? Sorting each column separately would break the rows apart, so Eli’s name could end up next to Ben’s score and section.
order() does not rearrange the data. It only computes the new row positions. Because you apply that one set of positions to every column at once with students[order(students$score), ], all columns move together and each row stays intact.

Question#8

```{r}
rank(scores)
cbind(scores, rank = rank(scores))
```
rank() uses ties.method = "average". Ben and Dex are tied for the top two positions (ranks 6 and 7), so each gets the average of those positions: (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5. This keeps the sum of all ranks consistent (1 + 2 + … + 7 = 28) and treats tied values fairly. Neither one is given a better position than the other. Because rank 1 is the lowest score here, the highest score gets the biggest ranks, which is why they land near 7 and not 1.

```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  employee   = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)
```
```{r}
sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales
```
```{r}
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Question#9

No, order() alone could not do both jobs. order() only tells you where each row should go to produce a sorted display. It gives you a rearrangement, not a standing. After using it, nothing in your data says that someone is 1st, 2nd, or 3rd.
rank() is the missing piece. It gives every item its own standing score and handles ties: Sam and Tin both get 1.5 because they sold the same amount. order() would simply put one of them above the other, even though they are equal. So rank() answers “what place is each person in?” and order() answers “in what sequence should I list them?”. You need rank() to award the ranks and order() to display the table in that sequence.
